'''Randy Thornhill'''{{DEFAULTSORT:Thornhill, Randy}} (born 1944) is an American [[entomologist]] and [[evolutionary biologist]]. He is a professor of [[biology]] at the [[University of New Mexico]], and was president of the [[Human Behavior and Evolution Society]] from 2011 to 2013.<ref name="springer" /> He is known for his evolutionary explanation of [[rape]] as well as his work on insect mating systems and the [[parasite-stress theory]].<ref name="watters">{{cite news | author = Watters, Ethan | date = 3 March 2014 | title = The Germ Theory of Democracy, Dictatorship, and All Your Most Cherished Beliefs | work = Pacific Standard | access-date = 21 March 2015 |url = https://psmag.com/social-justice/bugs-like-made-germ-theory-democracy-beliefs-73958}}</ref>

== Life ==

Thornhill was born in [[Alabama]] in 1944.<ref name="born">{{cite book |author1=Thornhill, R. |author2=Fincher, C. L. | year = 2014 | title = The Parasite-stress Theory of Values and Sociality | publisher = Springer | page = viii |isbn=9783319080406 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=WUYqBAAAQBAJ&pg=PR8}}</ref> When he was 12, his mother introduced him to [[Charles Darwin]]'s ''[[The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex]]'', which encouraged his later interest in human evolution.<ref name="salmon">{{cite AV media | people = Salmon, Catherine; Thornhill, Randy | title = HBES Interview Series - Randy Thornhill | work = Human Behavior an Evolution Society Founders Videos | publisher = YouTube | url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wsUb6Oy4NhU}}</ref>

He received a [[Bachelor of Science|BS]] in [[Zoology]] from [[Auburn University]] in 1968, an [[Master of Science|MS]] in entomology from Auburn University in 1970, and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in Zoology from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1974. His doctoral thesis discussed the [[evolutionary ecology]] of [[Mecoptera]] insects.<ref name="cv">{{cite web | author = Thornhill, R. | date = January 2015 | title = Curriculum Vitae | url = http://biology.unm.edu/Thornhill/rthorn.htm | access-date = 21 March 2015 | archive-date = 19 March 2015 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150319035125/http://biology.unm.edu/Thornhill/rthorn.htm | url-status = dead }}</ref> He was formerly married to fellow researcher Nancy Thornhill.<ref>{{cite news | author = Rosenfeld, Megan | date = 20 February 2000 | title = Rape a natural behavior? Theory causes an unnatural uproar | newspaper = The Washington Post | access-date = 21 March 2015 | url = https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20000220/4005841/rape-a-natural-behavior-theory-causes-an-unnatural-uproar}}</ref>

== Work ==

Thornhill's interests lie in the evolution and ecology of animal social psychology and behavior, as well as [[human behavioral ecology]] and [[evolutionary psychology]].<ref name="cv" /> In 1983, Thornhill published ''The Evolution of Insect Mating Systems'', a book that journalist [[Ethan Watters]] described as "groundbreaking".<ref name="watters" /> He considers this his most important work.<ref name="salmon" /> As of 2014, he has published four books and over 150 papers, which have been cited more than 17,000 times.<ref name="springer">{{cite book | author = Springer | year = 2014 | title = The Parasite-Stress Theory of Values and Sociality: About the authors | publisher = Springer.com | access-date = 21 March 2015 | url = https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783319080390}}</ref> His work has been featured in many newspapers, magazines, television shows and radio programs,<ref name="cv" /> including an interview on ''[[The Today Show]]''.<ref name="watters" />

Together with anthropologist Craig T. Palmer, Thornhill authored ''[[A Natural History of Rape]]'' in 2000. Thornhill and Palmer proposed that rape should be understood through evolutionary psychology,<ref name="Human Sexuality" /> and criticized the argument that rape is not sexually motivated.<ref name="Rape">{{cite book |first1=Randy|last1=Thornhill|first2=Craig T.| last2=Palmer| title = A Natural History of Rape: Biological Bases of Sexual Coercion |url=https://archive.org/details/naturalhistoryra00thor |url-access=limited | publisher = [[MIT Press]] | location=Cambridge, Massachusetts| year = 2000 | pages = [https://archive.org/details/naturalhistoryra00thor/page/n143 126], 133–135, 138–139|isbn=9780262201254 }}</ref> They argue that the capacity for rape is either an [[adaptation]] or a byproduct of adaptive traits such as sexual desire and aggressiveness.<ref name="Human Sexuality">{{cite book |first1=Simon|last1=LeVay |first2=Janice|last2=Baldwin |title=Human Sexuality, Third edition |year=2009 |publisher=[[Sinauer Associates, Inc.]] |location=Sunderland, Massachusetts| pages=598, 602 |isbn=978-0-87893-424-9}}</ref> The work provoked a major controversy. Thornhill received several death threats, and was assigned a campus police officer to escort him to and from class.<ref name="watters" /> A compendium of academic criticism was published,<ref>{{cite book |first=Cheryl Brown | last=Travis| year = 2003 | title = Evolution, Gender, and Rape | publisher = [[MIT Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts}}</ref> to which Thornhill responded.<ref>{{cite journal | first1 =Craig T. |last1=Palmer|first2=Roger|last2=Thornhill| year = 2003 | title = A posse of good citizens brings outlaw evolutionists to justice. A response to ''Evolution, Gender, and Rape''. Edited by Cheryl Brown Travis. (2003). Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. | journal = Evolutionary Psychology | volume = 1 | pages = 10–27 |article-number=147470490300100102 | doi = 10.1177/147470490300100102 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Since 2005, Thornhill has proposed that many human values evolved to protect against [[pathogen]]s.<ref name="springer" /> He believes that morality, political systems and religion are all influenced by regional variations in pathogen levels. In particular, Thornhill and colleagues have suggested that [[Collectivism and individualism|collectivism]] and [[xenophobia]] serve to ward off infectious disease. In support of this, they reported that collectivist cultures had a higher prevalence of pathogens than [[Individualism|individualist]] ones. Thornhill has also suggested that pathogen defense could help explain civil and ethnic warfare, homicide, [[patriarchal]] family structures, and social suppression of female sexuality.<ref name="watters" />

In 2021, Thornhill appeared as a guest on episode 38 of season 4 of the [[Jordan Peterson|Jordan B. Peterson]] Podcast entitled: ''Death, Disease, and Politics''. There, he discussed his research and views with the host (Peterson) about a range of topics, including [[physical attractiveness|attractiveness]], Thornhill's [[parasite-stress theory]], and the “critical role that [[Infection|infectious disease]] plays in humanity, [[Intelligence quotient|IQ]], [[Human sexuality|sex]], [[religion]], and [[conservatism]]”.<ref>{{Citation|last=FM|first=Player|title=S4E38: Death, Disease, and Politics {{!}} Dr. Randy Thornhill|url=https://player.fm/episodes/298360257|language=en|access-date=2021-07-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=S4E38: Death, Disease, and Politics {{!}} Dr. Randy Thornhill|url=https://www.thinkspot.com/online_content/jordan-peterson/s4e38-death-disease-and-politics-dr-randy-thornhill/vKu5mM/Event|access-date=2021-07-29|website=www.thinkspot.com}}</ref>
